## Why a separate entry point

The CATCHER cassette is unchanged, but Parse puts it in a different place and
builds the cell barcode differently, so neither `catcheR_10Xcatch()` nor
`catcheR_pipcatch()` can read these libraries.

|  | 10X | PIPseq | Parse |
|---|---|---|---|
| cassette on | read 2 | read 2 | **read 1**, reverse complement |
| cell barcode on | read 1, fixed 16 nt slice | read 1, four tiers with phasing | read 2, three ligation rounds |
| needs a whitelist | no | no | **yes** |
| molecular index | 12 nt UMI | 3 nt, not deduplicable | 10 nt UMI |

The real UMI is the most consequential difference. On PIPseq every metric is a
read count; on Parse `UMIxUCI` is a genuine molecule count, which is why the
Parse defaults can afford `UMI.count = 1` and a per-cell floor.

## Read layout

Read 1, after one leading base:

```
[1 nt] rc(reference 23) rc(UCI 6) rc(barcode 8) ACGCGTAGCTCGCTGATCAG ...
```

Read 2:

```
[UMI 10][bc3 8][ATGAGGGGTCAG][bc2 8][TCCAACCACCTC][bc1 8][poly-T]
```

The rounds run 3-2-1 from the 5' end because round 3 ligates last. Each 8 nt
slot is drawn from a published whitelist, so a slot that matches nothing is a
sequencing error rather than a new cell.

The cassette is sliced relative to the **vector constant**, not the reference.
Roughly 5% of cassette-bearing reads carry an error inside the 15 nt reference
anchor; anchoring on the constant recovers them with the correct barcode, while
the reads this also admits carry no valid barcode and are dropped at the
reference lookup.

## The barcode file is required

`barcode.data` must be split-pipe's own `barcode_data.csv`. Round 1 holds
**two** sequences per well, one oligo-dT and one random hexamer, both mapping
to the same well. In a 3' enrichment library the hexamer barcodes are
several-fold rarer, so a whitelist taken from the most abundant sequences per
round recovers only the dT set. On a real library, using the inferred
whitelist corrected 93% of reads; the real file corrected 99%.

The file is not a plain CSV - `#` comment lines separate the rounds and the
single header sits after the first of them - so `read.csv()` fails on it.
`catcheR_parsecatch()` reads it for you.

## A complete run

```r
library(catcheR)

res <- catcheR_parsecatch(
  folder         = "analysis_EB/scratch",
  fastq.read1    = c("AB019c_BC_n1_S7_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz",
                     "AB019c_BC_n2_S8_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz"),
  fastq.read2    = c("AB019c_BC_n1_S7_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz",
                     "AB019c_BC_n2_S8_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz"),
  sublibraries   = c("s1", "s2"),
  barcode.data   = "barcode_data.csv",
  barcodes.genes = c("rc_barcodes_genes_set1.csv", "rc_barcodes_genes_set2.csv"),
  set.names      = c("set1", "set2"),
  set.sizes      = c(100L, 60L),
  output_dir     = "analysis_EB/Output",
  sample_name    = "AB019c")
res
#> <parsecatch> sample AB019c | 21,451,610 read pairs over 2 sublibraries | ...
```

One FASTQ pair per sublibrary. Parse reuses well combinations across
sublibraries, so the same triplet in two of them is two different cells; the
sublibrary suffix is part of the cell ID for exactly that reason.

## Filtering, empty cells, and the matrix

```r
flt <- catcheR_parse_filtercatch(res, UMI.count = 1, percentage = 15,
                                 ratio = 2, min.cell.UMI = 20)
noc <- catcheR_parse_nocatch(res, filtered = flt)

obj <- catcheR_parse_seurat(
  res, filtered = flt, empty = noc,
  mtx   = "analysis_EB/scratch/count_matrix.mtx.gz",
  genes = "analysis_EB/scratch/all_genes.csv.gz",
  cells = "analysis_EB/scratch/cell_metadata.csv.gz",
  rename = TRUE, subset.valid = TRUE)
```

`count_matrix.mtx` is stored **cells x genes**, the transpose of the 10X and
PIPseeker convention, so `Seurat::ReadMtx()` cannot read it;
`catcheR_parse_seurat()` transposes on load. Cells are keyed by `bc_wells`,
which is what `catcheR_parsecatch()` emits, so the join is a plain string
match.

## Choosing the thresholds

Do not choose them by yield. Maximising the number of cells that get a call
argues for no filter at all; what the filter is for is keeping the calls
correct.

```r
acc <- catcheR_call_accuracy(res, min.truth.UMI = 100)
```

This takes the deep, unambiguous cells as ground truth, subsamples each one to
a target depth, re-applies the rule, and separates a *wrong* call from *no*
call. On a real library the share of calls made that were wrong ran 13% at
5 UMIs per cell, 9% at 10, 1.9% at 20 and 1.1% at 30 - which is what sets the
floor at 20.

```r
sw <- catcheR_threshold_sweep(res, percentage = c(10, 12, 15, 18, 20),
                              UMI.count = c(0, 1), min.cell.UMI = c(0, 20))
```

The sweep separates the two opposite ways a cell fails: no UCI cleared the cut,
or more than one did. Lowering `percentage` mostly moves cells from the first
into the second rather than into a call, which is why 12 is not an improvement
on 15 despite what the share distribution suggests by eye.

Watch for one arithmetic effect: a cell holding fewer than `100 / percentage`
UMIs has every single-UMI UCI clearing the percentage cut, so several pass and
the cell is rejected. At `percentage = 15` that is any cell under about
7 UMIs, and `UMI.count = 1` removes most of it.

## The honest denominator

The barcodes this pipeline produces include ambient ones that split-pipe never
called as cells. A detection rate over all observed barcodes overstates
coverage - sometimes severalfold. Quote the rate over the called-cell list,
which is what `catcheR_parse_seurat()` reports.
